The afternoon sunlight streams through the stained-glass window, gilding the rim of the silver platter like dripping, rich honey. The girl stands before the long table, gingerly holding her breath—as if the slightest lapse in focus might blow away the sweet feelings tucked deep in her heart like powdered sugar.
Is the cream too sweet? Is the jam too tart? Is the baked sponge too soft? Does the decoration look forced? Even though she has already used the finest ingredients in the world, she still cannot help but worry—worrying that her racing heart, like a rejected parcel, might be left sitting forever in a dusty corner of the room.
"Right here... would this be the perfect spot?"
She hesitates, unable to choose one place out of countless possibilities, as though locked in a heated board game where she just cannot bring herself to make the next move.
The Starborn pays no heed to the dreamlike, exquisite confection, simply watching her—her soft hair, the tips of her ears tinged a faint pink, and the way she steals unconscious glances toward the Starborn even while trying to stay careful.
The moment their eyes meet, she looks back flustered, afraid her feelings might be all too obvious, yet unwilling to stop halfway now. The setting sun grows brighter still, tree shadows swaying faintly outside the window. And that cake, crafted from the finest ingredients, rests quietly upon the table, baking the whole room into a sweet, gentle space.
The Starborn thinks: what she is decorating isn't sugar or cream at all. It is a girl's heart, lovingly adorned, that she is gently trying to offer to the Starborn.
1518850:
Char knows that Roiley loves the stars.
By day, Roiley looks especially proud. Before the winds on the training grounds have even settled, it raises its head high and shakes off the motes of light clinging between its wings—as if sharp turns, steep dives, and long-distance flights were nothing at all. When young knights draw too near, it lets out a soft snort and turns its head away, showing only a cool, aloof profile.
Yet when night falls and starlight fills the meadow, it walks of its own accord to the hill with the clearest view, folds its wings, and comes to a halt amid the blossoms and evening dew.
It has always been this way, for as long as she can remember.

Tonight, the stars seem brighter than usual. Roiley's spirits are lighter too, like a headwind met mid-flight.
Sensing something, Char follows its gaze—and sees someone walking through the night, toward this starlit grassy hill.
A gentle smile naturally blooms in the girl's eyes.

"Good evening, Starborn."
"If you'd like, won't you watch the stars with me?"
1518851:
As night's darkness blankets the lake, the shadows of the sea of trees and the tower sink into stillness as well. The breeze carries a faint chill off the water, stirring the deep-violet tips of the girl's hair.
She stands alone upon the shore with poised grace, her back straight. The shattered moonlight across the water drapes around her like sheer silk, as though she were born to stand equal alongside that noble, pristine radiance.
Yet this, too, is just an ordinary night.
Ever the picture of perfection, she has honed her etiquette, her speech, her stride, and even the way she casts her gaze until not a single flaw remains. Ever the picture of perfection, she can even temper her own brilliance as needed—so that when she stands before her future subjects, they can look directly upon her benevolence and grace.
She gazes up at the night sky and confides in the Starborn.
"I will inherit my duties, inherit the crown, and inherit every fate set before me. To do that, I must be graceful enough, wise enough, and strong enough."
Slowly, she draws her rapier. Its silver-white blade reflects the moonlight alongside the lake's surface.
She points the tip toward the vault of heaven. The ring of the steel is as clear as the echo of an oath. "I won't merely hold Hakuon's glory aloft upon a crown—I will engrave it into the name of every single one of my people."
Standing sword in hand, she gazes toward the distant future to which her blade points, then pivots and steps forward. Her footwork is precise and flowing, and the blade moves lightly, tracing crisp arcs of cold brilliance above the lake.
The Starborn has watched her dance with her sword countless times—by lakesides, beneath trees, before temples, along the roadside. Countless fragments of light glinting off her blade-tip flash through the Starborn's mind, while her gentle voice echoes endlessly in their ears—
"Wake up."
"Why are you sleeping in a place like this?"
As the girl leans down to ask, the deep-violet tips of her hair tickle the Starborn's forehead, with stars scattered across the night sky behind her.
At that moment, the Starborn can no longer tell whether it had all been a dream, or whether she had truly danced with her blade right here.
1518852:
I always dream of that day.
The flames in the dream make no sound, and the ruins hold no warmth. Only a suffocating fog rises from between the crumbling walls, swallowing everything I once knew bit by bit.
So much time has passed since then, yet the same scene keeps returning before my eyes, reminding me over and over—I couldn't protect the village. I couldn't protect everyone. Even continuing to live felt like some inexplicable mistake.

Perhaps that's why I was always afraid to venture far away.
Inside the coffin, it's cramped and dark. Still, it feels safer than the outside world. If I curl up inside, I don't have to think about terrifying questions like "what should I do from here on?"
So long as I guarded those buried memories, I felt as though I could pretend time wasn't moving forward and hold onto this small sliver of peace.

Lately, though, even that peace has begun to waver.
The dreams grow clearer and clearer, churning up my memories and flooding my mind all at once. Even sleep started to feel like a punishment. I told myself I just needed to endure a little longer—that I was already used to it, that I'd be fine bearing it alone.
And yet, Starborn, you looked so worried.
I tried to brush it off like I always do, but I couldn't fool those eyes. Under your earnest gaze, it felt pointless to put up a front. So I followed you outside—to the sanatorium, to the mines, and to face once more the one place I feared approaching most of all.

Truthfully, I've been scared the whole time.
Scared of those memories, of the fog, of being swallowed whole by the past if I ever stopped moving. Scared even more by the fact that my duty is over, yet I'm still here—not knowing where to go, or whether someone like me even deserves to move forward.
Sinking into a deep sleep and stopping all thought might be so much easier. If I just fell asleep like this, would I finally stop being afraid?

But you came after me, Starborn.
You told me you were worried. You told me there are still so many beautiful things in this world. You even offered to look for them with me.

Yes... this life was left to me with everyone's blessing. It doesn't have to exist solely for atonement, or solely to guard ruins and keepsakes. It's okay to see different sights—to reach out toward that "future" I was once too afraid to even imagine.

Starborn, I am still scared.
Still, if you will stay by my side... if those words weren't just a passing whim... if, whenever I grow timid and halt again, you will reach out your hand to me just like today—then I think I will try moving forward.
Even if it's only a single step, I want to walk out into that world you spoke of, filled with so many beautiful things.
1518853:
The wind is very light. Windel likes that.
Windel sees a wood elf standing there.
Pulls the bow. Looses an arrow. Direct hit.

But the wood elf doesn't smile.
The wood elf pulls the bow again. Looses another arrow. Another direct hit.
Still, the wood elf doesn't smile.

Windel flies in a circle around the wood elf.
Smells like leaves. Smells like trees.
And smells just a tiny bit grumpy, too.

After that, the wood elf's friend arrives.
The wood elf and the friend talk a lot, then go to a place where lots of wind blows.
It is a very nice place.
The grass sways. The leaves sway. Long hair sways, too.
The wood elf closes her eyes.
The wood elf's friend closes theirs, too.
The wood elf's friend falls asleep.

The wood elf asks Windel to watch over the friend.
That is very easy. Windel helps.
Windel can tell that the wood elf's friend made the grumpy smell go away.

The wood elf's friend wakes up and watches the wood elf standing there. Pulls the bow. Looses an arrow.
As the arrow flies, the wind makes a big sound and seems very happy.
Different from before.

The wood elf and the friend talk a lot.
Windel doesn't really understand.
But Windel sees the wood elf smile.

Windel thinks: this is good.
Yes, this is good.
1518854:
Month X, Day X — Sunny

Today, I went to the Fleece Market with the Starborn.

Originally, I had only meant to pick up a few local specialties on my day off, but the moment we stepped into the market, all the colorful goods caught my eye. Before I knew it, I was carrying several paper bags in my hands. The Starborn laughed and asked, "Didn't we buy a little too much?"—yet never once showed a hint of annoyance, patiently keeping me company the whole time.
I did make a careless mistake today, though. I mixed up the time to pick out tea leaves at the Tianjiang Chamber of Commerce with the time to pick up books at the bookstore. Fortunately, the Starborn volunteered to help. Being helped out like this makes me feel like I don't have to do everything on my own, and that maybe it's okay to take things a little easier.

After that, we also visited a plushie shop. It was even livelier than I had imagined. The wooden shelves were lined with all kinds of plushies—some looking proud, some looking wonderfully blank. Some were so charming that just looking at them naturally brought a smile to my face.
That was where I found an Umi plushie. Seeing it reminded me of another plushie from long ago—one I used to sleep beside, that always eased my worries.
That plushie was full of memories, and it had watched over me as I grew up. Even though it had grown old and worn ages ago, I had never once thought of buying a new one.

Today, however, was different.
When I hugged this Umi plushie, what came to mind wasn't the past, but today. The bustling streets, how the Starborn wandered from stall to stall with me, chatting outside the bookstore, the quiet flutter of excitement as we stepped into the plushie shop together... Perhaps a new plushie can hold new memories too.

Still, I only noticed after getting back home... I must have hugged it a bit too tightly today, because two of its seams came undone.
To tear it even slightly right after bringing it home—how clumsy of me.

Still, though... if I'm going to fix it, maybe I could use that as an excuse to invite the Starborn back to the Fleece Market one more time.
1518855:
To my future self, someday:
I don't know when you'll read this letter. Maybe you'll be sorting your packs on a journey, or maybe you'll already be back home. Or maybe... just like me right now, you'll have just finished training.
Come to think of it, after training today, I had the most delicious cake. The cream was rich, the fruit was refreshing... My shoulders were stiff and sore from practice, yet the moment I took a bite, I couldn't help feeling happy.
At first, I meant to mind my manners and savor it slowly, you know? But before I knew it, I'd accidentally gotten some on my face. It was a little embarrassing, though the person eating with me said, "You don't have to be so stiff when you're taking a break."
...I guess that's really what it's all about, huh.
Lately, I've been starting to understand little by little. The real strength that keeps you moving forward isn't just duty, responsibility, or honor. Instead, it's the smaller, ordinary things... a tasty meal, a training session safely finished, an interesting person you happen to meet, sweets shared together... and the belief that even if you fall, you can always get back up again.
So, future me, if you ever realize you're walking too fast and forgetting to enjoy the scenery along the way, stop and take a little rest. Order a slice of cake, take your time eating it, and don't worry if you get a bit on your face.
And remember that little apprentice knight who left home for the very first time—too nervous to sleep, yet brimming with anticipation. She wasn't braver than anyone else, but she never once gave up trying to grow.
I hope you're still the same.
—From Lily, still in training
1518856:
Dear Grandpa Chief,
Good morning! Did you sleep well last night? May the ancestral spirits watch over you. By the time you read this letter, I'll probably be up on the mountain tilling the fields.
Yesterday, while patrolling the forest, I found a patch of land super rich in Karama. Wild medicinal herbs were growing everywhere, and after gathering for a long while, I filled up my little basket. Even now, my fingers still smell of plant sap that won't wash out.
It's damp, quiet, and gets just the right amount of sunlight. I want to clear it right away and turn it into Charlulu Village's herb field, so I think I'll be up on the mountain all day today. Trouble is, I haven't laid out the herbs I sorted last night to dry yet. Could you tell Big Sis for me? Tell her to set the little basket of herbs outside to dry when the sun is strongest today, and not to forget to bring them back inside before sunset. Otherwise... I'm holding Big Sis responsible and making her cook dinner tonight!
Even after restocking the village's medicine supply, I still have plenty of herbs left over, so I'm going to use them for experiments. I want to research potions that can solve everyone's everyday troubles—like a potion to make you taller, Chief, or a potion to help Big Sis learn to read. Wouldn't it be amazing if someday, no matter what someone wished for, just one sip of Luruka's medicine could make it come true? Everyone would surely live so much happier!
So I'd love for you and Big Sis to help me test my potions again. Keep this a secret from Big Sis for now, okay? Otherwise, she'll get scared and hide in the mountains again.
1518857:
Lan Xiangzi bustled about all day preparing to leave the underground.
She pulled out her best-preserved outfit and pasted fresh talismans onto it. Finally, she wiped down her coffin three more times. With that done, Lan Xiangzi sat down beside the coffin and stared off into space for a while.
She had never traveled far. Even as a child, the farthest she had ever strayed from the village was the riverbank behind the hill. Later, after the village was buried underground, she could not even visit the riverbank anymore.
She began to wonder where she was supposed to go. It had been far too long since she last thought about such a thing. Until now, she had always known what she had to do: patrol the perimeter every morning and evening, check the jade disc for any abnormalities, sweep the offering altar clean, and keep watch. Day after day passed just like that. Now, suddenly, she no longer had to guard it—and instead, she found herself at a loss as to what she should do.
...In any case, she ought to pack first. Making up her mind, she stood and opened the coffin, only to think for a moment and close it again.
Best to sort out her clothes first after all. She took out an old robe she had saved from long ago and began mending its frayed cuffs. Halfway through sewing, however, she suddenly paused. "Do folks in the outside world... still wear clothes like these?"
...She didn't know. She had been cut off from the outside world for far too long.
Did people outside no longer use copper coins?
Would others think a coffin was strange?
Might someone suddenly strike up a conversation with her?
If someone greeted her, would she have to reply?
What should she even say back... "Hello"?
Lan Xiangzi slowly crouched down and hugged her knees, steam beginning to rise from her head. Just then, however, she suddenly thought of that person—the one called the "Starborn."
Maybe the things she was worrying about weren't all that important. And even if they were... she could just ask the Starborn.
After all, that person would be right by her side from now on.
Lan Xiangzi sat back down beside her coffin and gazed up at the underground "sky" devoid of sun or moon, waiting for tomorrow.
Just like that little girl guarding the formation so many moons ago—frightened, yet unable to keep from hoping.
1518858:
In the eastern outskirts of Jinghua Prefecture lies a peach grove. Every blossoming season, a steady stream of visitors comes to admire the trees stretching for miles. Hanging throughout the grove are countless peach blossom talismans wishing for peace, renown, or a good marriage, for everyone says that a sincere heart can move the immortal fox dwelling within.
There was once a woodcutter named Zhao Sheng. In his early twenties, he was poor and owned no household possessions to speak of. His father had passed away early, leaving him and his mother to rely on one another. Neighbors urged him to settle down and marry soon, yet Zhao Sheng always shook his head and refused. When asked why, he would only say, "I still have an elderly mother to care for—there is no need to burden someone else with hardship." All who heard this admired his character.
Yet Zhao Sheng's mother worried over her son's marriage prospects and went to the peach grove often to pray. Every five days, without fail, she would bring incense, candles, and handmade flaky pastries to the grove and hang a single peach blossom talisman on a tree. Written upon it were just a few words: "May my son find a good match."
When Zhao Sheng found out, he was at a loss and could only take them down in secret. One would be hung up and he would take it down; another would be hung up and he would take it down again, over and over.
One day, returning from chopping wood, he happened to pass through the peach grove and caught sight of a young girl beneath a tree. Dressed in pink, she sat leaning against a peach tree, flipping through several peach blossom talismans in her hands as she read them. Beside her sat a familiar box of flaky pastries, half-eaten. Drawing closer, he saw that the talisman she had spread open was none other than one written by his own mother—and he heard the girl mutter under her breath, "This one again?"
Startled, Zhao Sheng stepped forward to ask her about it. The girl looked up at him and asked instead, "Are you Zhao Sheng?"
Zhao Sheng was even more taken aback. Before he could question her further, the girl had already rolled up the talisman and smiled sweetly, saying, "So this is what you look like." No sooner had she spoken than she rose to her feet, flicked her sleeves, and vanished deep into the peach grove in the blink of an eye. Zhao Sheng chased after her for several paces, but she was already nowhere to be seen.
Upon returning to the village, he told his neighbors what had happened. Some dismissed it as mere daydreaming and others laughed that his eyes had played tricks on him, though one old man whispered, "Perhaps there truly is an immortal fox living in that peach grove."
Zhao Sheng had never believed in the supernatural, yet after that day he spotted the girl in the peach grove several more times. Sometimes she would lie on her stomach along a branch, flipping through peach blossom talismans; other times she would hold a sweet pastry, watching passersby as she ate. Whenever he tried to approach, however, she would once again vanish without a trace.
Several years passed in this way, and thanks to Zhao Sheng's diligent labor, his household's fortunes gradually improved. His mother still went to the peach grove to pray for good fortune, though she no longer brought up his marriage every single day.
Toward the end of spring one year, someone came visiting from a neighboring village. Having heard of Zhao Sheng's diligence and filial piety, a family there had come to propose a marriage.
A few months later, the match was finally settled. On the wedding day, Zhao Sheng's mother was overjoyed and went out of her way to prepare a generous offering of flaky pastries to give thanks at the peach grove, with Zhao Sheng accompanying her. Though the peach blossoms were blooming as beautifully as ever, there was no sign of the immortal fox—only a single unfamiliar peach blossom talisman hanging from the tip of a branch. The characters on the paper were slightly uneven: "Zhao Sheng's match is now set. With this, my debt is repaid." Below it, a single line had been added in smaller script: "The flaky pastries were delicious." And where a signature would go on the talisman, a clumsy little fox had been drawn.
Seeing this, Zhao Sheng could not help but burst out laughing. Looking back, he saw the shadows of blossoms swaying deep within the peach grove, and for a brief moment he thought he heard the faint chime of a bell and a girl's laughter carried on the wind. He strained his ears to listen once more, yet nothing was there.
In the years that followed, Zhao Sheng was blessed with children and grandchildren, and every spring when the peach trees bloomed, he would bring his family to the grove. And whenever anyone asked him about the immortal fox, Zhao Sheng would always smile and reply, "Perhaps there truly is an immortal fox living in that peach grove."
1518859:
What is a fated bond?
Tracing the mere definition of the word never quite explains it. A chance encounter, the guiding hand of destiny, gazes briefly meeting the moment you turn around—everyone uses this word to describe moments that defy pure reason. And we believe that some connections in this world are not born without cause, but are quietly woven together by some gentler force.
Yet rather than vaguely dismissing everything as "decided by destiny," we might do better to search for the small, tangible things where a fated bond actually takes root.

Ears of golden wheat symbolize abundance, clodimes wealth, and mokyuns guidance—it may seem self-evident, yet if you think about it, it was never that way from the beginning.
Meaning is not a label stuck onto an object. It is something bestowed little by little through repeated touch, use, remembrance, and hope.
A symbol is nothing more than the result of what a heart chooses to believe.
Surely a fated bond is the same.

It need not be anything so grand as the will of heaven.
If someone gazes upon it, understands it, and gives it meaning, even an ordinary scene begins to shine softly within memory.
Call it a "chance meeting," an "unforgettable encounter," a "heaven-sent match," or "destiny"—what makes it a true bond is that the two people standing here right now wish to believe together in the meaning it holds.

So perhaps a fated bond is—
when one person raises a hand to make flowers bloom in an illusion, and the other watches with earnest eyes.
In that very moment, an unseen thread has already been quietly tied.
1518860:
Medicine Receipt Confirmation

Recipient: Cathbelle
Deliverer: Starborn
Delivery Method: Hand-delivered in person
Condition of Medicine: Bottle intact. No damage or leakage.
Receipt Status: Received
Dosage Status: Taken
Additional Notes:
The deliverer entered the recipient's room without sufficient prior notice, constituting a clear breach of procedure. However, given that they appeared to be rushing with the medicine out of concern for my health rather than any intent to show disrespect, no further action will be taken.
Furthermore, I must clarify my own condition here. What was described as "looking pale" is merely temporary fatigue and warrants no excessive reaction from others.
...That said, if I am to record the circumstances truthfully, there is one detail I cannot omit.
When I stated that there was no need to show such concern for someone who is merely a maid, the Starborn said that station does not matter.
They were neither flowery words nor spoken in a formal tone. Precisely for that reason, they felt all the more sincere—an unvarnished truth spoken straight from the heart.
At first, I assumed it was merely a remark made on impulse.
Yet even after delivering the medicine, the Starborn did not leave at once, staying until they had seen me drink it and rest properly before finally seeming relieved. Honestly, that behavior was... a little bothersome.
Only a little bothersome, mind you.
Had anyone else overstepped so abruptly, I would surely have felt nothing but displeasure.
Yet when it is the Starborn, I do not mind it.
Perhaps it is because such unmistakable fluster and care do not look like something easily feigned. Or perhaps it was because, when they looked at me like that, I thought for the very first time that one need not always maintain the distance of "how things ought to be"—


(Note: At the bottom of the page remains a short, unfinished stroke of ink. It seems the writer suddenly realized something, set down the brush, and never added another word.
In the end, this receipt confirmation was neatly folded and tucked away in the deepest drawer of Cathbelle's desk.)
1518861:
"The Tale of the Forest Goddess of Charlulu Village"
The village's old hunter once said that in the deepest part of the dense forest dwells a goddess, living in a place where flowers grow taller than the trees.
With a gentle wave of her hand, nurturing rain falls upon the grass and blossoms. They say she can converse with Chicchi and even help wounded Chameleus stand once more.
Every Kibo longed to meet her and hoped to earn her favor.

The first was Duru. It thought that if it could run faster than anyone else, the goddess would surely like it best.
So it practiced running every day, sometimes even sneaking into Charlulu Village to steal fish just to sharpen its getaway speed.
As a result, on the day it raced toward the goddess's dwelling, it ran far too fast and plunged straight off a cliff into a valley, never getting to meet her at all.

The second was Frogure. It thought that if it could sing better than anyone else, the goddess would surely like it best.
So it practiced singing every day. It sang beneath the trees, by the lakeside, and up toward Tana in the night sky.
As a result, it ruined its throat, and its once-lovely "popo, ribbit" turned into a raspy "gaa-gaa" croak.

The third was Granzaros. It thought that if it were the strongest of all, the goddess would surely like it best.
So it trained its strength every day. It hauled boulders, rammed tree trunks, lifted fallen deadwood, and shoved sleeping monoliths.
As a result, when it charged headlong into a mountain cliffside, it brought the rocks crashing down and buried itself beneath the shattered stones.

Realizing none of these methods worked, the Kibo decided to bring gifts to the goddess instead.
Before long, more and more Kibo joined in—some carrying flowers in their mouths, some offering fruit, some gathering sparkling stones, and some even catching glowing bugs.
Day after day they journeyed deep into the forest, until at last a graceful Fawndy spoke up. "You fools. When has the goddess ever accepted a single gift?"
Indeed, she had taken none of the flowers, none of the fruit, and none of the stones.
The Fawndy continued.
"Yet she planted the flowers in her garden, buried the fruit seeds in the soil, and arranged the stones along the brook."
"Even for that glowing bug, she found a cozy new nest, didn't she?"
And so the Kibo finally understood. The Forest Goddess plays no favorites—she loves everything within the forest.
She is just like the rain that falls upon the woods and the sunlight that warms the valley.
So long as each of them simply lives as itself, the Forest Goddess will always watch over them.
And whenever they weave between the trees, the Kibo always feel her gentle gaze quietly watching over them from that place where flowers grow taller than the trees.
1518862:
The most important part of clockwork craft is constant refinement.
To Han Youyou, "completion" is merely the starting point for the next improvement. A genius mind is never content with the status quo; with a single spark of inspiration, an entire design is reborn anew.
Even her prized Clockwork Kite naturally has endless room for improvement!

This time, determined to push its flight performance even higher, she unusually stayed cooped up quietly in her workshop for several days, tweaking and adjusting it over and over. At last, she built something extraordinary.
"Watch closely, Starborn! This is my finest work yet!"

With a roar and a burst of flame, the Clockwork Kite soared into the sky at breathtaking speed, whipping the tips of the girl's hair upward in the rush of wind.
"It still can't carry a person yet, though, so borrow a Kibo's strength and fly alongside it! That still counts as a stroll in the sky together, right?"
Han Youyou cheered in excitement. Everything was going swimmingly—save for the faint, sudden snap that rang out...

"—Oh, oh no! The Clockwork Kite's handle... it broke!"
Oh dear, failures are part and parcel of invention.
Not to worry—a master of clockwork never lets setbacks stop her from trying again!
1518863:
"Personal: To the 'Polaris of the Night Sky'"
"Tonight, when Starmy stretches, please come to the loftiest height of Fleece."
"Allow me to show you the magic of the moon."
Closing the invitation infused with the sweetness of candy, beneath the pitch-black curtain of night, Fleece was still brightly lit with glowing lamps. Yet its residents must already be fast asleep, making the quiet stand out all the more. The crisp clack of high heels echoed as a girl came to meet the appointment. Warm orange light traced the edges of her face and kindled a gleam in her amber eyes, though tonight the sky was overcast and moonless.
"Right on time." There was not the slightest hint of disappointment in the girl's voice. "Even I'd be in a bind if my sole audience member didn't show up," she added, a proud look spreading across her face at seeing the Starborn arrive as promised—the very expression she wore whenever she was about to showcase her talents.
"Hmph! I know what you're worried about. The Wicked King of Pitch Black must have plucked the moon away with his sinful hands, right? But a little hiccup like that is child's play for this 'Crimson Flame-Light of Swift Thunder'!" The girl spread her arms wide before the Starborn, her red coat fluttering in the breeze.
"Besides, I have you. 'Polaris of the Night Sky'—no matter how deep the darkness others sink into, you can always stand unyielding and shine with the light of hope."
"Watch me. Lend me your strength, and let me breathe life into this night once more."
The girl stood just ahead, with the curtain of night pressing close around them.
"Behold—the Arcane Rite of the Moon!"
As the clouds and mist were gently swept aside by the wind—like a handmaiden softly drawing back the curtains to help a princess peek outside—a pure, cool white radiance softened the girl's silhouette, almost melting her into the overwhelmingly enchanting full moon behind her.
When had the chorus of insects begun to sing?
"That's not all, you know." The girl raised her left hand and held it beside her eye. A wisp of thin cloud drifted past, and the mysterious light within her eyes shone brighter still.
"This is the magic of the moon." The tips of her hair and hat reflected the moonlight, making the motes of dust drifting in the air stand out all the more clearly. The wind stilled, the clouds ceased to move, and the unseen insects seemed ready to sing on until the end of breathtaking eternity.
Time... was the town still even there?
"Right now, in this moment... it feels like you and I are the only ones left in the whole world..."
Rubina's eyes gleamed in the moonlight, and at that instant, the clock tower bell tolled three times.
"That concludes tonight's show. Thank you all for watching."
The girl gave a theatrical bow to her surroundings.
"Next time, I'll bring you an even more splendid program. Look forward to it!"
1518864:
"Ladies and gentlemen! Welcome to today's show. Today's guest is—Starmy of Fading Light!"
"Any friend who keeps a Kibo knows how it is. These little companions who spend every day and night with us each have their own charms: their earnest gaze when they spot delicious food, the drowsy swaying when they're sleepy, the pure, innocent smiles when they're happy. Every little thing they do tugs right at our heartstrings."
"Of course, when they make a silly little blunder, we're undoubtedly the first ones to burst out laughing. Sometimes we even pull a harmless prank on a Kibo we've Starlinked with just to see them get a bit flustered—and gladly take whatever tiny retaliation they dish back."
"And now, our next act—Starmy of Fading Light, vanquished at the hands of Crimson Flame-Thunder!"
"Look! Starmy of Fading Light struts proudly forward. The jewel on its chest sparkles brightly, having absorbed plenty of starlight. What graceful poise, what an elegant stride! Yet all of this is about to be shattered by the wicked Crimson Flame-Thunder! She leaps out suddenly from the corner, startling this poor little creature—"
"Rubina? What are you muttering about?"
"Eek?! P-Polaris of the Night Sky?! How long have you been standing there?!" Jolted straight out of her daydream, the girl panicked, trying to explain herself, though her thoughts refused to come together right away.
"C-Come on... shh..." First, the girl urged the Starborn to keep their voice down.
"Meow!" Yet feline Kibo are always especially sharp. "O wicked crimson shadow, how long have you been lurking there—what sinister scheme are you plotting!"
"Looks like she was trying to scare you."
"N-No, I wasn't... I didn't..." Rubina, however, had completely forgotten to lower the hands she'd curled like sharp claws.
"Hmph! Alas for you, your scheme has ended in failure! Now it is Crimson Flame-Thunder who stands in disarray. Truly, good and evil reap what they sow, meow." Starmy of Fading Light strolled up to the Starborn's feet and gracefully licked its forepaw.
"...Polaris of the Night Sky, Starmy of Fading Light—were you two in cahoots?! Since when did you team up?!"
"A triumph of justice, meow. Let's go." Tracing a neat arc with the tip of its tail, it walked off, leaving the stunned girl sitting on the ground, blushing furiously as she watched her two dear friends stroll away into the distance.
"Huh...?"
"Ladies and gentlemen, evildoers always meet their just deserts. Crimson Flame-Thunder serves as a prime example. Let this be a lesson to you all!"
1518865:
The forest holds a stillness that makes you want to soften your footsteps.
Afternoon light filtered through the branches and leaves, scattering finely across soil and moss. Even when a breeze passed through, it only swayed the treetops gently, waking the faintest rustle of leaves. In a place like this, there is no need for words. Simply walking slowly brings a gradual calm to the heart.
Except...

"Awoo? Awooo!"
"You don't have to shiver anymore. I'm coming to save you right now... M-Moo?!"
A rather startled cry rang out through the quiet woods.

Somehow, a young snow wolf had climbed up onto a branch and was stuck, unable to go forward or back. A girl with cow horns was doing her utmost to edge closer with great care.
The branch trembled and creaked precariously as if it might snap at any second, yet she refused to give up.
Still, when you reached out a hand from beneath the tree, she seemed even more flustered by it than by the fragile branch.

Before long, the girl made it safely back to the ground with the snow wolf in tow—
with a racing heartbeat and flushed cheeks to match.

1. If you find yourself repeatedly insisting "I'm not sick" upon admission, please rest assured.
Miss Anis has already included that symptom in her routine observation checklist.

2. If Miss Anis determines that treatment is necessary, please refrain from refusing whenever possible.
Refusing will not change her diagnosis—it will only prolong the time until you stop putting up a brave front.

3. Before treatment, you may feel nervous upon seeing the instruments.
This is a normal reaction. Please close your eyes and wait for Miss Anis's gentle voice to clear up any misunderstandings.

Usually, this is proof of Miss Anis's steady skill and the ample patience with which she is caring for you.

Especially when Miss Anis is smiling as she looks at you.

When Aiples first hit the market, I remember Peipei buying a few. Yet she hadn't walked far before coming right back, returning one to the stall to swap it for a smaller one.
I asked her, "What's wrong? Was that Aiple bruised?" She shook her head, hesitated for a moment, and said, "Everyone always buys the bigger ones, so this little Aiple won't get sold. I felt sorry for it..."
I nearly burst out laughing. Then I patted the little Aiple in Peipei's hands and pressed the big Aiple she'd just returned back against her chest. "You can have this one too."
After thinking for a moment, I added, "I'll leave taking care of these little ones to you, alright? I'll look after the rest of the Aiples!"
Peipei gave me a serious nod, and that look on her face was just adorable.
—Massima, Greengrocer

Whenever Peipei visits my shop, she usually doesn't buy anything. She doesn't seem interested in finely polished gems, preferring instead to stand quietly in front of the raw stones for a while.
One time, she was staring intently at a raw stone that had just arrived. It hadn't been polished yet and looked quite plain.
When I asked Peipei what she liked about it, she thought for a moment and answered slowly, "I don't know... but it seems kind of interesting."
I wanted to hear more, but she was already drawn away by someone calling out Pepe Candy for sale, leaving me standing alone in front of that raw stone, lost in thought for half the day. What on earth did Peipei find interesting about it?
—Gladia, Jeweler

That day, I had just finished making a new candy recipe and wanted someone to taste-test it. Peipei happened to be walking past the shop, so I stepped out with the candy to greet her.
She must have thought I was trying to sell her something, because she shook her head. I hurriedly explained it didn't cost anything—it was just a sample.
Peipei looked down at the candy, then up at me, and finally asked in a small voice, "If it's a sample, does that mean I have to tell you what I think after eating it?"
Amused, I told her yes.
So Peipei popped one of the candies into her mouth and stood right there chewing quietly for a while, before suddenly asking with a very serious expression, "Grandpa Shine, if Peipei says it doesn't taste good, will you be sad?"
To be honest, at my age, my sense of taste has dulled a bit. Sometimes the new recipes I try really don't turn out as hoped.
Yet everyone in town is someone I've watched grow up, so they always shower me with praise to save my pride. Then, when I actually put a new item on sale, hardly anyone buys it.
Peipei's words were a rare, sincere evaluation—more precious to me than any flattery.
Afterward, I gave Peipei a bag of candy as thanks. One of the classic flavors already proven popular on the market, of course.
—Shine, Candy Shop Owner
1518869:
I believe the most important part of a maid's work is "taking action beforehand."
Waiting until one's master asks is already too late. A truly capable maid notices dust before it settles, deals with foul odors before they spread, and eradicates pests before they can build a nest. That way, the master never has to be bothered by trivial matters.
To achieve this, keen observation, initiative, and decisiveness are all indispensable.
For instance, when cleaning a room, I first identify where dirt tends to accumulate and tidy up in order. If anything blocks my view, it must be lifted or moved aside; otherwise, every corner cannot be thoroughly cleaned. It isn't difficult—a bit of strength and patience is plenty.
What do I mean by "a bit"?
Oh, just shifting a wardrobe and lifting the sofa while I'm at it. I can do that with one hand, so it hardly warrants special explanation.
Furthermore, I believe being tidy means more than merely being "free of dust."
Is the storage intuitive? Are items easy to retrieve? Do the curtains drape in neat curves? Are the edges of the bedding smoothed of wrinkles? Every single detail must be checked. A maid's competence shows in a room's comfort as well. Someone who can't even fluff a pillow properly isn't worth mentioning.
As for pests, my motto is always a swift, decisive strike.
Giving them time to struggle only creates unnecessary trouble. Before the master's attention is diverted, it is best to finish them quickly, quietly, and thoroughly. With the right tool, one blow is usually enough. Even if an unsightly mark is occasionally left behind, a little time spent cleaning it up solves the problem completely.

Cleaning, organizing, removing stains, maintaining the environment, attending to the master's daily needs—everything I do is simply what a maid is expected to perform.
...Excuse me?
Ordinary maids don't lift obstructive furniture along with the floor tiles underneath?
Is that so?
Wait—then how else are you supposed to eradicate the dirt and pests?
